claim: Nematostella vectensis uses nematocytes to detect and capture prey using stinging cells.
source: Jellyfish, sea anemones, and hydrozoans of the Cnidarian phylum use specialized cells called cnidocytes to facilitate both sensation and secretion required for prey capture and defense (Watson and Mire-Thibodeaux, 1994b).

claim: Two major types of cnidocytes contribute to prey capture by the tentacles of Nematostella vectensis: spirocytes and nematocytes.
source: Two major types of cnidocytes contribute to prey capture by the tentacles of the starlet sea anemone (Nematostella vectensis, Figure 1A): (1) spirocytes, anthozoan-specific cells that extrude a thread-like organelle to ensnare prey, and (2) nematocytes, pan-cnidarian cells which eject a single-use venom-covered barb to mediate stinging (Babonis and Martindale, 2017).

claim: Spirocytes are anthozoan-specific cells that extrude a thread-like organelle to ensnare prey.
source: Two major types of cnidocytes contribute to prey capture by the tentacles of the starlet sea anemone (Nematostella vectensis, Figure 1A): (1) spirocytes, anthozoan-specific cells that extrude a thread-like organelle to ensnare prey, and (2) nematocytes, pan-cnidarian cells which eject a single-use venom-covered barb to mediate stinging (Babonis and Martindale, 2017).

claim: Nematocytes are pan-cnidarian cells which eject a single-use venom-covered barb to mediate stinging.
source: Two major types of cnidocytes contribute to prey capture by the tentacles of the starlet sea anemone (Nematostella vectensis, Figure 1A): (1) spirocytes, anthozoan-specific cells that extrude a thread-like organelle to ensnare prey, and (2) nematocytes, pan-cnidarian cells which eject a single-use venom-covered barb to mediate stinging (Babonis and Martindale, 2017).

claim: Nematocyst discharge occurs at an acceleration of up to 5.41 × 10^6 g, among the fastest of any biological process.
source: Sensory cues from prey act on nematocytes to trigger the explosive discharge of a specialized organelle (nematocyst) at an acceleration of up to 5.41 × 106 g, among the fastest of any biological process (Holstein and Tardent, 1984; Nüchter et al., 2006; Figure 1B).
evidence: Cited from Holstein and Tardent, 1984; Nüchter et al., 2006

claim: The nematocyst can only be discharged once.
source: The nematocyst can only be discharged once and therefore stinging represents an energetically expensive process that is likely tightly regulated (Watson and Mire-Thibodeaux, 1994b, Babonis and Martindale, 2014).
evidence: Cited from Watson and Mire-Thibodeaux, 1994b, Babonis and Martindale, 2014

claim: Simultaneously presented chemical and mechanical (chemo-tactile) cues are required to elicit nematocyte discharge.
source: Indeed, simultaneously presented chemical and mechanical (chemo-tactile) cues are required to elicit nematocyte discharge (Pantin, 1942a; Watson and Hessinger, 1989; Watson and Hessinger, 1992; Anderson and Bouchard, 2009).
evidence: Cited from Pantin, 1942a; Watson and Hessinger, 1989; Watson and Hessinger, 1992; Anderson and Bouchard, 2009

claim: Electrical stimulation of nematocytes increases the probability of discharge in a calcium (Ca2+)-dependent manner.
source: Electrical stimulation of nematocytes increases the probability of discharge in a calcium (Ca2+)-dependent manner (Anderson and Mckay, 1987; McKay and Anderson, 1988; Santoro and Salleo, 1991; Gitter et al., 1994; Watson and Hessinger, 1994a; Anderson and Bouchard, 2009), but direct recordings from nematocytes are limited and thus mechanisms by which environmental signals control discharge are not well studied.
evidence: Cited from Anderson and Mckay, 1987; McKay and Anderson, 1988; Santoro and Salleo, 1991; Gitter et al., 1994; Watson and Hessinger, 1994a; Anderson and Bouchard, 2009

claim: Nematocytes exhibit voltage-gated inward currents that are activated by positive or depolarized membrane voltages.
source: Using intracellular cesium (Cs+) to block potassium (K+) currents revealed a voltage-gated inward current that was activated by positive or depolarized membrane voltages (ICaV, Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from patch clamp recordings shown in Figure 1C

claim: Nematocyte voltage-gated currents (ICaV) begin to inactivate at voltages more negative than could be technically measured.
source: Remarkably, ICaV began to inactivate at voltages more negative than we could technically measure, thus demonstrating an unusual voltage sensitivity of this conductance (Figure 1C,D).

claim: Neuronal voltage-gated currents had a lower threshold for activation and exhibited much weaker voltage-dependent inactivation compared to nematocytes.
source: Neuronal voltage-gated currents had a lower threshold for activation and exhibited much weaker voltage-dependent inactivation (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D), similar to currents found in neurons of other animals (Hille, 2001), indicating that nematocytes exhibit unusual voltage-dependent properties.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D, and cited from Hille, 2001

claim: ICaV is a Ca2+-sensitive current.
source: Ion substitution and pore blocker experiments confirmed ICaV is a Ca2+-sensitive current (Figure 1E,F), consistent with the contribution of extracellular Ca2+ to chemo-tactile-induced discharge (Watson and Hessinger, 1994a; Gitter et al., 1994; Figure 1G).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F,G and cited from Watson and Hessinger, 1994a; Gitter et al., 1994

claim: Increased concentrations of extracellular Ca2+ did not affect inactivation of ICaV.
source: Increased concentrations of extracellular Ca2+ did not affect inactivation of ICaV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting the enhanced voltage-dependent inactivation is intrinsic to the channel complex.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: The enhanced voltage-dependent inactivation of ICaV is intrinsic to the channel complex.
source: Increased concentrations of extracellular Ca2+ did not affect inactivation of ICaV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting the enhanced voltage-dependent inactivation is intrinsic to the channel complex.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing Ca2+ concentration does not affect inactivation

claim: ICaV renders nematocytes completely inactivated at typical resting membrane voltages.
source: This observation is important because it suggests ICaV renders nematocytes completely inactivated at typical resting membrane voltages and thus cells could not be stimulated from resting state.

claim: The orthologue of cacnb2, a β subunit of CaV channels, was the highest expressed CaV transcript in nematocyte-enriched cells, with levels 14-fold higher than other cells in the sea anemone.
source: The orthologue of cacnb2, a β subunit of CaV channels, was the highest expressed CaV transcript in nematocyte-enriched cells, with levels 14-fold higher than other cells in the sea anemone (Figure 2A).

claim: β subunits only interact with α subunits of high voltage-activated (HVA) calcium channels.
source: Importantly, β subunits only interact with α subunits of high voltage-activated (HVA) calcium channels (Perez-Reyes, 2003).

claim: There is significant enrichment for cacna1a, the pore-forming subunit of HVA CaV2.1, and high expression of cacna2d1 in nematocyte-enriched cells.
source: In agreement with robust β subunit expression, we found significant enrichment for cacna1a, the pore-forming subunit of HVA CaV2.1, and high expression of cacna2d1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Specific expression of cacna1a in nematocytes of sea anemone tentacles has been previously reported.
source: These observations are consistent with a previous report demonstrating specific expression of cacna1a in nematocytes of sea anemone tentacles and expression of β subunits in nematocytes from jellyfish (Bouchard et al., 2006; Moran and Zakon, 2014; Bouchard and Anderson, 2014).
evidence: Cited from Bouchard et al., 2006; Moran and Zakon, 2014; Bouchard and Anderson, 2014

claim: Expression of cacna1h was observed at lower levels and across all cells.
source: Expression of cacna1h, which does not interact with auxiliary subunits (Buraei and Yang, 2010), was also observed, albeit at lower levels and across all cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and cited from Buraei and Yang, 2010

claim: Heterologously-expressed nCaV channels inactivated at very negative voltages with an estimated Vi1/2 = -101.5 ± 1.6mV.
source: Heterologously-expressed nCav channels (Nematostella cacna1a, cacnb2, cacna2d1) inactivated at very negative voltages (estimated Vi1/2 = -101.5 ± 1.6mV, n = 5) versus mammalian orthologues (mCaV, Vi1/2 = -20.9 ± 3.4mV, n = 10).

claim: Mammalian CaV orthologues (mCaV) have a Vi1/2 = -20.9 ± 3.4mV.
source: Heterologously-expressed nCav channels (Nematostella cacna1a, cacnb2, cacna2d1) inactivated at very negative voltages (estimated Vi1/2 = -101.5 ± 1.6mV, n = 5) versus mammalian orthologues (mCaV, Vi1/2 = -20.9 ± 3.4mV, n = 10).

claim: Apparent activation thresholds were the same for nCaV and mCaV: nCaV Va1/2 = -9.8 ± 0.3mV, mCaV Va1/2 = -10.4 ± 0.5mV.
source: Apparent activation thresholds were the same: nCaV Va1/2 = -9.8 ± 0.3mV, n = 5, mCaV Va1/2 = -10.4 ± 0.5mV, n = 9.

claim: nCaV exhibited slow inactivation with −70 mV holding potential that was best fit by two exponential functions with time constants of 10.0 and 369.5 s.
source: nCaV exhibited slow inactivation with −70 mV holding potential (0.2 Hz stimulation, 5 s inter-pulse interval) that was best fit by two exponential functions with time constants of 10.0 and 369.5 s. n = 6, multiple row two-tailed student's t-test with significance of p<0.05 by 15 s and p<0.0001 by 500 s.

claim: nCaV inactivated at −40 mV and quickly recovered at negative holding potentials.
source: nCav inactivated at −40 mV and quickly recovered at negative holding potentials. n = 7 for nCaV, n = 6 for mCaV.

claim: The mCaV β subunit drastically shifted nCaV inactivation by ~56 mV in the positive direction.
source: In this case, the mCaV β subunit drastically shifted nCaV inactivation by ~56 mV in the positive direction, prevented complete inactivation, and produced slower fast inactivation (Figure 2E–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2E–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: nCaV β was sufficient to confer greatly enhanced voltage-dependent inactivation to mCaV.
source: Furthermore, nCaV β was sufficient to confer greatly enhanced voltage-dependent inactivation to mCaV (Figure 2E,G).

claim: nCaV β, the most enriched CaV subunit in nematocytes, confers nCaV's uniquely-sensitive voltage-dependent inactivation.
source: From these results, we conclude that nCaV β, the most enriched CaV subunit in nematocytes, confers nCaV's uniquely-sensitive voltage-dependent inactivation.

claim: Nematocytes had a resting potential of −64.8 ± 8.9 mV.
source: Under our conditions, nematocytes had a resting potential of −64.8 ± 8.9 mV and did not produce a voltage spike when injected with current from rest (Figure 3A).

claim: Nematocytes did not produce a voltage spike when injected with current from rest.
source: Under our conditions, nematocytes had a resting potential of −64.8 ± 8.9 mV and did not produce a voltage spike when injected with current from rest (Figure 3A).

claim: When nematocytes were first hyperpolarized to −90 mV and subsequently stimulated by current injection, they produced a singular long voltage spike.
source: Consistent with this idea, when nematocytes were first hyperpolarized to −90 mV and subsequently stimulated by current injection, we observed a singular long voltage spike (Figure 3B,C).

claim: Tentacle neurons produced multiple narrow spikes when injected with equivalent current amplitudes from a similar resting voltage.
source: In contrast, tentacle neurons produced multiple narrow spikes when injected with equivalent current amplitudes from a similar resting voltage, consistent with other neural systems (Figure 3A–C).

claim: Strong voltage-dependent inactivation prevents nematocyte activation from rest.
source: Furthermore, these results indicate strong voltage-dependent inactivation prevents nematocyte activation from rest.

claim: Nematocytes exhibited transient outward K+ currents that quickly inactivated.
source: Nematocytes exhibited transient outward K+ currents that quickly inactivated, while neurons had large sustained K+ currents, perhaps important for repolarization and repetitive spiking (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: Neurons had large sustained K+ currents, perhaps important for repolarization and repetitive spiking.
source: Nematocytes exhibited transient outward K+ currents that quickly inactivated, while neurons had large sustained K+ currents, perhaps important for repolarization and repetitive spiking (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C and speculation about function

claim: The transient component of the nematocyte K+ current was highly sensitive to voltage-dependent inactivation, similar to ICaV.
source: The transient component of the nematocyte K+ current was highly sensitive to voltage-dependent inactivation, similar to ICaV (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: The transient K+ current in nematocytes was abolished by the rapid intracellular Ca2+ chelator BAPTA or by removing external Ca2+.
source: This K+ current was abolished by the rapid intracellular Ca2+ chelator BAPTA or by removing external Ca2+, similar to the effect of the K+ channel blocker TEA+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: Nematocyte-enriched cells expressed numerous Ca2+-activated K+ channels.
source: Consistent with this observation, nematocyte-enriched cells expressed numerous Ca2+-activated K+ channels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Transcriptomic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: Using intracellular Cs+ to block K+ currents resulted in prolonged voltage spikes and greatly increased resting membrane voltage.
source: Furthermore, using intracellular Cs+ to block K+ currents resulted in prolonged voltage spikes and greatly increased resting membrane voltage, substantiating a role for K+ channels in modulating membrane voltage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G

claim: The deflection of isolated nematocyte cnidocils elicited a mechanically gated inward current with rapid activation and inactivation kinetics.
source: Indeed, we found the deflection of isolated nematocyte cnidocils elicited a mechanically gated inward current with rapid activation and inactivation kinetics.
evidence: Experimental data from mechanical stimulation experiments

claim: The mechanically gated inward current in nematocytes was abolished by gadolinium (Gd3+).
source: This current was abolished by gadolinium (Gd3+), which blocks mechanoreceptor and other cation channels, and was not observed in neurons (Figure 4A–C).

claim: Nematocyte-enriched cells differentially expressed transcripts encoding NompC (no mechanoreceptor potential C).
source: Furthermore, nematocyte-enriched cells differentially expressed transcripts encoding NompC (no mechanoreceptor potential C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), a widely conserved mechanoreceptor previously found to localize to the cnidocil of nematocytes from Hydra (Schüler et al., 2015).
evidence: Transcriptomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and cited from Schüler et al., 2015

claim: Heterologous expression of Nematostella NompC (nNompC) resulted in a mechanically-gated current with similar properties to native nematocytes, including rapid kinetics and Gd3+ sensitivity.
source: Heterologous expression of Nematostella NompC (nNompC) resulted in a mechanically-gated current with similar properties to native nematocytes, including rapid kinetics and Gd3+ sensitivity (Figure 4A–C).

claim: nNompC had similar rapid kinetics, Gd3+ sensitivity, pressure-response relationships, and nonselective cation conductance compared to Drosophila orthologue (dNompC).
source: Comparison with the Drosophila orthologue (dNompC) demonstrated nNompC had similar rapid kinetics, Gd3+ sensitivity, pressure-response relationships, and nonselective cation conductance, all consistent with the conservation of protein regions important for mechanosensitivity and ion selectivity (Jin et al., 2017; Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D, and cited from Jin et al., 2017

claim: Nematocytes are intrinsically mechanosensitive.
source: Thus, we conclude nematocytes are intrinsically mechanosensitive and suggest nNompC contributes to nematocyte mechanosensitivity.

claim: nNompC contributes to nematocyte mechanosensitivity.
source: Thus, we conclude nematocytes are intrinsically mechanosensitive and suggest nNompC contributes to nematocyte mechanosensitivity.
evidence: Inferred from expression and functional data

claim: Prey-derived chemicals did not elicit electrical responses from isolated nematocytes.
source: While prey-derived chemicals (<3 kDa extract from brine shrimp) evoked robust behavioral responses, similar treatments did not elicit electrical responses from isolated nematocytes (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Only acetylcholine (ACh) elicited a significant response from isolated nematocytes among well-conserved neurotransmitters screened.
source: To test this possibility, we screened isolated nematocytes for responses to well-conserved neurotransmitters and found only acetylcholine (ACh) elicited a significant response (Figure 4D,E).

claim: ACh-evoked outward currents in nematocytes were abolished by nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) antagonists and recapitulated by nicotine.
source: ACh-evoked outward currents were abolished by nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) antagonists and recapitulated by nicotine (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F

claim: The K+ channel blocker TEA+ and the intracellular Ca2+ chelator BAPTA inhibited ACh-evoked responses in nematocytes.
source: The K+ channel blocker TEA+ and the intracellular Ca2+ chelator BAPTA inhibited responses, suggesting ACh elicits K+ channel activity downstream of increased intracellular Ca2+.

claim: ACh elicits K+ channel activity downstream of increased intracellular Ca2+ in nematocytes.
source: The K+ channel blocker TEA+ and the intracellular Ca2+ chelator BAPTA inhibited responses, suggesting ACh elicits K+ channel activity downstream of increased intracellular Ca2+.

claim: Blockade of K+ currents with intracellular Cs+ revealed an ACh-elicited inward current that was enhanced by increased extracellular Ca2+ and blocked by the nAChR antagonist mecamylamine.
source: While the G-protein signaling inhibitor GDPβS did not affect outward currents, blockade of K+ currents with intracellular Cs+ revealed an ACh-elicited inward current that was enhanced by increased extracellular Ca2+ and blocked by the nAChR antagonist mecamylamine (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H

claim: ACh evokes a Ca2+-permeable nAChR-like signaling pathway to engage Ca2+-activated K+ channels in nematocytes.
source: These results suggest ACh evokes a Ca2+-permeable nAChR-like signaling pathway to engage Ca2+-activated K+ channels, consistent with the absence of muscarinic ACh receptors in Nematostella (Faltine-Gonzalez and Layden, 2019).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited from Faltine-Gonzalez and Layden, 2019

claim: Nematocyte-enriched cells expressed numerous nAChR-like transcripts which had well-conserved domains involved in Ca2+ permeability.
source: In agreement with this observation, nematocyte-enriched cells expressed numerous nAChR-like transcripts which had well-conserved domains involved in Ca2+ permeability (Fucile, 2004; Figure 4—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Transcriptomic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I,J and cited from Fucile, 2004

claim: There is robust acetylcholinesterase activity in tentacles.
source: Finally, we found robust acetylcholinesterase activity in tentacles, further suggesting a role for ACh signaling in nematocyte function (Figure 4G).

claim: Nematocytes use cholinergic signaling to regulate K+ currents, similar to how efferent cholinergic innervation of vertebrate hair cells modulates nAChR-K+ channel signaling to inhibit auditory responses.
source: These results demonstrate that nematocytes use cholinergic signaling to regulate K+ currents, similar to how efferent cholinergic innervation of vertebrate hair cells modulates nAChR-K+ channel signaling to inhibit auditory responses (Elgoyhen and Katz, 2012).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and cited from Elgoyhen and Katz, 2012

claim: Each nematocyte exhibited a long process that extended into the ectoderm.
source: Interestingly, each nematocyte exhibited a long process, of presently unknown function, that extended into the ectoderm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Dense core vesicles were localized to electron-dense regions at the junction between each nematocyte and one other cell type, either sensory neurons or spirocytes.
source: Importantly, dense core vesicles were localized to electron-dense regions at the junction between each nematocyte and one other cell type, either sensory neurons or spirocytes (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–E

claim: Nematocytes receive synaptic input from both neurons and spirocytes.
source: Thus, nematocytes receive synaptic input from both neurons and spirocytes and likely serve as a site for integrating multiple signals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: Inferred from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F,G

claim: Nematocytes likely serve as a site for integrating multiple signals.
source: Thus, nematocytes receive synaptic input from both neurons and spirocytes and likely serve as a site for integrating multiple signals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F,G).

claim: Cnidarians can simultaneously discharge multiple cnidocyte types to most efficiently capture prey.
source: This observation is consistent with the ability of cnidarians to simultaneously discharge multiple cnidocyte types to most efficiently capture prey (Pantin, 1942a).

claim: ACh induced hyperpolarization of nematocytes.
source: ACh induced hyperpolarization of nematocytes. n = 6, p<0.01 paired two-tailed student's t-test.

claim: Depolarizing current injection did not induce active properties from rest, but did elicit a voltage spike from most nematocytes hyperpolarized by ACh.
source: Depolarizing current injection did not induce active properties from rest, but did elicit a voltage spike from most nematocytes hyperpolarized by ACh. n = 6, p<0.01 paired two-tailed student's t-test.

claim: Chemo-tactile-induced nematocyte discharge was inhibited by the mechanoreceptor current blocker Gd3+.
source: Chemo-tactile-induced nematocyte discharge (touch + prey extract, n = 8) was inhibited by the mechanoreceptor current blocker Gd3+ (n = 7) and nAChR antagonist mecamylamine (n = 14).

claim: Chemo-tactile-induced nematocyte discharge was inhibited by the nAChR antagonist mecamylamine.
source: Chemo-tactile-induced nematocyte discharge (touch + prey extract, n = 8) was inhibited by the mechanoreceptor current blocker Gd3+ (n = 7) and nAChR antagonist mecamylamine (n = 14).

claim: Touch + ACh was sufficient to induce nematocyte discharge in the absence of chemical stimulation.
source: In the absence of chemical stimulation (touch - prey extract, n = 5), touch + ACh (n = 14) was sufficient to induce discharge, which was inhibited by mecamylamine (n = 12).

claim: The requirement for prey-derived chemicals was completely recapitulated by ACh.
source: Moreover, the requirement for prey-derived chemicals was completely recapitulated by ACh (Figure 5D).

claim: The unique ICaV voltage-dependent inactivation provides a mechanism by which nematocytes filter extraneous depolarizing mechanical signals.
source: Thus, we propose that the unique ICaV voltage-dependent inactivation provides a mechanism by which nematocytes filter extraneous depolarizing mechanical signals, but can integrate chemosensory-induced hyperpolarization together with a depolarizing stimulus to elicit robust signal amplification and discharge responses (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and proposed model shown in Figure 6

claim: Nematocytes can integrate chemosensory-induced hyperpolarization together with a depolarizing stimulus to elicit robust signal amplification and discharge responses.
source: Thus, we propose that the unique ICaV voltage-dependent inactivation provides a mechanism by which nematocytes filter extraneous depolarizing mechanical signals, but can integrate chemosensory-induced hyperpolarization together with a depolarizing stimulus to elicit robust signal amplification and discharge responses (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and proposed model shown in Figure 6

claim: Nematocytes use the specialized properties of nCaV to filter salient chemo-tactile signals from environmental noise.
source: Here, we demonstrate that nematocytes use the specialized properties of nCaV to filter salient chemo-tactile signals from environmental noise.

claim: The involvement of Ca2+ signaling in nematocyte discharge is consistent with a well-established role for Ca2+ influx in mediating discharge across multiple cnidarian species.
source: The involvement of Ca2+ signaling in this process is consistent with a well-established role for Ca2+ influx in mediating discharge across multiple cnidarian species (McKay and Anderson, 1988; Santoro and Salleo, 1991; Watson and Hessinger, 1994a).
evidence: Cited from McKay and Anderson, 1988; Santoro and Salleo, 1991; Watson and Hessinger, 1994a

claim: It has been proposed that Ca2+ influx alters the permeability of the nematocyst capsule and/or initiates the rapid dissociation of ions within the cyst to induce osmotic changes within the organelle.
source: It has been proposed that Ca2+ influx alters the permeability of the nematocyst capsule and/or initiates the rapid dissociation of ions within the cyst to induce osmotic changes within the organelle (Lubbock and Amos, 1981; Lubbock et al., 1981; Weber, 1990; Tardent, 1995).
evidence: Cited from Lubbock and Amos, 1981; Lubbock et al., 1981; Weber, 1990; Tardent, 1995

claim: Nematocytes express multiple Ca2+ handling proteins.
source: Our transcriptomic analyses demonstrate that nematocytes express multiple Ca2+ handling proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–F), which could control Ca2+ signaling domains in response to spatially restricted sensory transduction cascades.
evidence: Transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–F

claim: Ca2+ handling proteins in nematocytes could control Ca2+ signaling domains in response to spatially restricted sensory transduction cascades.
source: Our transcriptomic analyses demonstrate that nematocytes express multiple Ca2+ handling proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–F), which could control Ca2+ signaling domains in response to spatially restricted sensory transduction cascades.

claim: CaV currents could mediate an increase of >500 µM Ca2+ considering a uniform distribution across the small cytoplasmic volume (5%) not occupied by the nematocyst.
source: Indeed, CaV currents could mediate an increase of >500 µM Ca2+ considering a uniform distribution across the small cytoplasmic volume (5%) not occupied by the nematocyst.

claim: Anatomical organization and pharmacological dependence for cellular and discharge activity in anthozoan nematocytes differs from hydrozoans.
source: For example, anatomical organization and pharmacological dependence for cellular and discharge activity in anthozoan nematocytes differs from hydrozoans (Anderson and Mckay, 1987; Kass-Simon and Scappaticci, Jr., 2002; Oliver et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Anderson and Mckay, 1987; Kass-Simon and Scappaticci, Jr., 2002; Oliver et al., 2008

claim: Nematocysts vary extensively in morphology, differing in the length of the extruded thread, the presence of spines, and the composition of toxins.
source: Indeed, nematocysts vary extensively in morphology, differing in the length of the extruded thread, the presence of spines, and the composition of toxins (Kass-Simon and Scappaticci, Jr., 2002), likely reflecting the diversity of organismal needs.
evidence: Cited from Kass-Simon and Scappaticci, Jr., 2002

claim: Numerous amino acids, lipids, and N-acetylated sugars can individually modulate nematocyte discharge.
source: In addition to chemical mixtures, such as prey extract, numerous amino acids, lipids, and N-acetylated sugars can individually modulate nematocyte discharge (Watson and Hessinger, 1992).

claim: Discharge can be regulated by organismal nutritional state.
source: Discharge can also be regulated by organismal nutritional state (Sandberg et al., 1971), suggesting nematocytes could receive input from digestive cells or hormones.
evidence: Cited from Sandberg et al., 1971 and speculation about mechanism

claim: The freshwater cnidarian, Hydra vulgaris, uses a specific cnidocyte to grasp surfaces for phototaxis.
source: For example, the freshwater cnidarian, Hydra vulgaris, uses a specific cnidocyte to grasp surfaces for phototaxis, suggesting that these cells could be regulated downstream of a photoreceptor (Plachetzki et al., 2012).

claim: Clownfish can live among the tentacles of sea anemones without harmful effects.
source: For example, clownfish can live among the tentacles of sea anemones without harmful effects, although the exact mechanism by which this occurs is unclear (Lubbock, 1980).

claim: Certain species of nudibranchs and ctenophores acquire undischarged nematocysts from prey and store them for later defense.
source: Certain species of nudibranchs and ctenophores acquire undischarged nematocysts from prey and store them for later defense, indicating that these organisms are able to initially prevent discharge responses (Greenwood, 2009).
